newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Shell launches youth training in Nigeria's Ogoni.
newsitem.headline: Shell launches youth training in Nigeria's Ogoni.

text.p: The Nigerian subsidiary of Royal Dutch Shell Group on Tuesday formally commissioned a scheme to train 366 youths in the volatile Ogoni oil-producing area of Nigeria, a company statement said.
Shell was forced to quit Ogoniland in 1993 over fighting between rival communities in the area.

"This is the first time since we pulled out of Ogoniland in 1993 that Shell staff have stood on Ogoni soil on Shell business," Shell's Nigerian deputy chief executive Egbert Imomoh said at the commissioning ceremony in Bori, Rivers state.
The 10-month programme will train the Ogoni youths in carpentry, welding, computer studies and soap-making to make them employable.
The announcement was made on the same day as news that fresh fighting between rival clans in the Niger delta had forced Shell to cut its Nigerian oil output by more than 10 percent.
Shell was criticised by enviromental pressure groups in 1995 when nine Ogoni minority rights activists including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa were hanged over the murder of four Ogoni chiefs.
The nine had been campaigning for self-determination for the 500,000-strong Ogoni tribe and compensation from Shell for ecological damage to the area from its oil activities.
Imomoh said Shell had no plans to resume oil output in Ogoniland, adding the company's priority was to help tackle the problems facing the Ogoni people where it could do so.

At the time it stopped operations in Ogoni, Shell was producing about 23,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the area, compared with its output in Nigeria of 950,000 bpd, almost half the country's total production.
